doc.title: Hal Galper interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 27, 2022

title: Composing by intuition and starting bands to solve musical problems
summary: Galper says he does not compose deliberately and formed bands to work out concepts such as pentatonics and cells, which took fifteen and ten years.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Okay. When you — after disposing of the Rhodes and you went back to a piano trio, did you have a different way of composing from before the experience, those two years? Did you sit and compose in a different way?

I don’t compose deliberately. It has to be an accident. I don’t force it. I love my intuition telling me what to do. If my intuition has a tune it’ll come up. I’ve got a tune I’ve been working on, fragments, gorgeous fragments, I’ve been trying to finish for a couple of years. Last night I was working on it and very frustrated. I couldn’t hear — I have found a resolution for it but I couldn’t find the notes. Just — it varies. Tunes are different animals. There are no two that are the same. You know, usually I wrote tunes to solve a problem, a musical problem. And I started a band. I started a lot of my bands for that reason because the apprenticeship system was going down the drain and I needed to play with really good people and keep playing you know, to keep my chops up and to keep growing. So quite often my bands and my writing were solutions to problem, musical problems. You know? If I was working on a new concept I would start a band, write the music for that concept that forced me to be in that concept and learn how to play in it, and that’s what happened with pentatonics you know? And cells you know. I just made myself a situation where I had to play that way. And I got it together. It took me fifteen years to get pentatonics together, and ten years to get cells together.
